Findings.Comment: The function comment states the caller's context bounds the operation, but the change replaces both uses of `ctx` with `context.Background()`. This means the caller cannot cancel the request via context, and the function may block indefinitely even if the context is canceled. Both the HTTP request creation (line 13) and the call to `getTextCapped` (line 18) must use `ctx`.
Findings.Headline: FetchDiff ignores caller's context, breaking cancellation
Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.
The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: When `r` is non-nil but `r.Ticket` is nil, the code falls through to the return statement which dereferences `r.Ticket.Key`. This will cause a runtime panic (nil pointer dereference) on every call with a nil ticket. The original code correctly returned `r.Body` in this case.
Findings.Headline: Nil pointer dereference when Ticket is nil
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: The condition change from `last > len(lines)` to `last >= len(lines)` combined with setting `last = len(lines) + 1` will cause an out-of-bounds slice access when `last` equals `len(lines)`. When `first + n == len(lines)`, the code now sets `last` to `len(lines) + 1`, but Go slice indexing `[first:last]` requires `last <= len(lines)`. This will panic at runtime.
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter out-of-bounds slice panic on boundary

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.
The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.
The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The commit's error return value is discarded. If `tx.Commit(ctx)` fails (e.g., due to serialization error, connection loss, or constraint violation), the function returns `nil` and the caller proceeds as if the claim was recorded, but the transaction is rolled back by the deferred `tx.Rollback`. This silently loses data and breaks the contract that a nil error means the claim is persisted.
Findings.Headline: Commit error ignored in AddClaim — silent data loss

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The diff swaps the error values in the two conditions, inverting the intended behavior described in the comment and variable name. The first condition (no rows) should wrap `ErrNoClaim` so callers can detect "no claim" via `errors.Is`, but now it wraps the raw `errNoRows`. The second condition (database errors) should wrap the original error for diagnosis, but now it wraps `ErrNoClaim`, masking faults as "no claim". This breaks the contract: callers using `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` will get false negatives for "no claim" and false positives for database errors.
Findings.Headline: Error values swapped in Owner: ErrNoClaim vs errNoRows

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
